This presentation summarises the technical report. The focus is not only on dashboard-style reporting, but on using visual analytics to discover distributional patterns and potential drivers of profitability and volatility.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Analytical objective

Explore numerical and categorical distributions.
Investigate factors associated with profitability.
Use visual evidence and statistical validation together.
Treat extreme losses as part of volatility, not noise to ignore.


The assignment asks for both univariate and bivariate visual analytics. I define profitability through profit and loss ratio, and volatility through spread, claim occurrence, and extreme incurred-loss behaviour.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Portfolio trend


Premium and incurred losses both increase from 2022 to 2024. The key question is whether premium growth is sufficient to absorb the increasing loss burden.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Loss ratio worsened in 2024


The 2024 loss ratio is visibly higher than 2022 and 2023. This points to declining profitability, assuming expenses are not separately modelled here.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Univariate: numerical skewness


The most important univariate pattern is claim zero-inflation and right skewness. Many records have no incurred loss, but a small number of records have very large loss ratios.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Univariate: categorical concentration


Policy mix and bonus-score mix are concentrated. This affects interpretation: a smaller category can have a high loss ratio, but it must be evaluated against exposure size.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Policy type and profitability


Comprehensive products, especially COMP_N, have the highest aggregate loss ratios. Third-party-only coverage has the lowest ratio in this comparison.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Volatility by policy type


The boxplot uses capped loss ratio to make the spread visible. The large right tail confirms that volatility is a material feature of this portfolio.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Other risk-related segments


Bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area all show visible differences in aggregate loss ratio. These are useful candidates for underwriting or pricing review.

title: Take-home Exercise 1

Implications

Review premium adequacy for comprehensive products.
Investigate 2024 deterioration in loss ratio.
Use bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area as segmentation checks.
Examine extreme losses separately from typical-policy behaviour.
Validate any pricing action with exposure and mix-adjusted modelling.


The visual analytics process identifies where to investigate next. It does not replace actuarial modelling, but it provides a clear evidence trail for prioritising portfolio questions.

pacman::p_load(plotly, ggtern, tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%")


#Reading the data into R environment
pop_data <- read_csv("../data/r4va/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv")


#Deriving the young, economy active and old measures
agpop_mutated <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(`Year` = as.character(Year))%>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8]))%>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16]))  %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21])) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24])) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018)%>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)


#Building the static ternary plot
ggtern(data=agpop_mutated,aes(x=YOUNG,y=ACTIVE, z=OLD)) +
  geom_point()









#Building the static ternary plot
ggtern(data=agpop_mutated, aes(x=YOUNG,y=ACTIVE, z=OLD)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title="Population structure, 2018") +
  theme_rgbw()









# reusable function for creating annotation object
label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt, 
    x = 0.5, y = 1.08,
    ax = 0, ay = 0,
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
    xanchor = "center",
    align = "center",
    font = list(family = "serif", size = 15, color = "white"),
    bgcolor = "#b3b3b3", bordercolor = "black", borderwidth = 2
  )
}

# reusable function for axis formatting
axis <- function(txt) {
  list(
    title = txt, tickformat = ".0%", tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

ternaryAxes <- list(
  aaxis = axis("Young"), 
  baxis = axis("Active"), 
  caxis = axis("Old")
)

# Initiating a plotly visualization 
plot_ly(
  agpop_mutated, 
  a = ~YOUNG, 
  b = ~ACTIVE, 
  c = ~OLD, 
  color = I("black"), 
  type = "scatterternary"
) %>%
  layout(
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"), 
    ternary = ternaryAxes,
    width = 750,
    height = 650,
    margin = list(l = 20, r = 20, b = 20, t = 80)
  )

The plus sign means another layer follows. Line 3: geom_bar() + — Counts how many students are in each category and draws one bar per category. The plus sign means another layer follows. Line 4: coord_flip() + — Flips the axes so the plot becomes horizontal instead of vertical. The plus sign means another layer follows. Line 5: theme_minimal() — Uses a simple minimal theme with fewer visual distractions.

1 Overview
This report applies visual analytics to a real-world Spanish motor insurance portfolio dataset from Mendeley Data. The portfolio contains policy-level transactions from 2022 to 2024, including policy attributes, premium components, claim counts, incurred losses, and exposure.
The analysis addresses two required tasks:

Univariate visual analytics: explore the distributions and characteristics of numerical and categorical variables.
Bivariate visual analytics: investigate and statistically validate factors associated with portfolio profitability and volatility.

For this report:

Profitability is represented by profit = total_premium - total_incurred and the aggregate loss ratio total_incurred / total_premium.
Volatility is represented by the spread and upper tail of individual policy loss ratios, claim occurrence, and high-incurred outliers.

Mid-age drivers and very old drivers show elevated aggregate ratios, while vehicle-age bands from 4 to 20 years appear less favourable than the oldest vehicle band. This indicates that underwriting interpretation should account for product mix and exposure, not age alone.


4.5 Brand-level volatility screen

brand_tbl <- motor |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    p95_loss_ratio = quantile(loss_ratio, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(exposure >= 1000)

brand_tbl |>
  ggplot(aes(x = claim_frequency, y = loss_ratio, size = exposure)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, colour = "#08519c") +
  geom_text(
    data = brand_tbl |> slice_max(loss_ratio, n = 8),
    aes(label = vehicle_brand), vjust = -0.8, size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Brand-level screen for high loss ratio and claim frequency",
    subtitle = "Only brands with exposure >= 1,000 are shown.",
    x = "Claim frequency", y = "Aggregate loss ratio", size = "Exposure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Draft interpretation to customise: This chart is a screening device rather than a final underwriting decision. Brands in the upper-right area combine higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio, making them candidates for deeper investigation.


4.6 Statistical validation
Because individual loss ratio is highly skewed and zero-inflated, non-parametric tests are used for group differences. The Kruskal-Wallis test is applied to the 99th-percentile-capped loss ratio. Chi-square tests are used to validate whether claim occurrence differs by segment.

test_vars <- c("policy_type", "bonus_score", "driver_age_band", "vehicle_age_band", "fuel_type", "circulation_area", "year")

kw_tbl <- map_dfr(test_vars, \(v) {
  kt <- kruskal.test(as.formula(paste("loss_ratio_cap ~", v)), data = motor)
  tibble(test = "Kruskal-Wallis", variable = v, statistic = unname(kt$statistic), p_value = kt$p.value)
})

chi_tbl <- map_dfr(test_vars, \(v) {
  ct <- chisq.test(table(motor[[v]], motor$claim_flag))
  tibble(test = "Chi-square", variable = v, statistic = unname(ct$statistic), p_value = ct$p.value)
})

validation_tbl <- bind_rows(kw_tbl, chi_tbl) |>
  mutate(p_value_label = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3)) |>
  select(test, variable, statistic, p_value_label)
